analysis.one_liner: Bans lawmaker stock trading, restricts the lobbyist revolving door, and creates public campaign financing.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to ten House committees two weeks before the session ended, the bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This sweeping package would rewrite federal ethics and campaign finance law: Members of Congress and senior officials would have to sell off individual stocks, former lobbyists would be barred from government jobs for years, a new Office of Public Integrity would enforce ethics rules, corporate PAC money would be banned, and Senate and presidential campaigns could run on public funding and small donations. It was introduced on December 20, 2022, thirteen days before that Congress expired, and died without any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want decisions made without the appearance that officials are trading on personal investments or future lobbying jobs. The bill's rules would apply to Members of Congress, the President, senior executive officials, and the lobbying and contracting industries that currently rotate personnel and money through government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters worried about conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: Bars former registered lobbyists from executive branch jobs for 2 years (6 years for corporate lobbyists) and imposes similar bans in congressional offices, with waivers that must be published and justified publicly.

Requires Members of Congress and senior government officials to divest individual stocks, bonds, derivatives, and hedge fund interests, permitting only diversified widely held funds, government bonds, and a new federal investment account.

Requires the President and Vice President to divest conflicting financial interests into blind trusts and disclose 8 years of tax returns, and bars the President from federal contracts beyond statutory limits.

Creates an Office of Public Integrity to enforce ethics laws across the executive and legislative branches, and extends the general conflicts-of-interest criminal law to the President, Vice President, and Congress.

Bans corporate PAC contributions and corporate fundraising for Members of Congress, bans foreign-owned corporations from spending on U.S. elections, requires disclosure of major donors to tax-exempt groups, and prohibits big-donor ambassador appointments.
Establishes public financing for Senate and presidential campaigns through a 'Freedom From Influence Fund,' with expanded small-dollar matching payments so candidates can run without large donors.

Imposes a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures, bans contingent-fee lobbying, and requires 'political intelligence' firms that sell government information to investors to register under lobbying law.

Extends the Freedom of Information Act to federal contractors, requires large contractors to publicly disclose their political spending, and creates a code of conduct and complaint process for federal judges including the Supreme Court.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms, large banks and corporations, federal contractors, and incumbent officials would bear the cost: longer hiring bans, divestment of holdings, disclosure of political spending, a tax on lobbying, and potential civil penalties up to a share of annual net profit for companies that violate hiring restrictions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lobbyists, big banks, contractors, and officeholders

drawbacks.text: The bill touches nearly every corner of government — it was referred to ten committees at once — making it far more complex than a focused stock-trading ban, and its breadth raised the odds that contested provisions would sink the whole package.

The divestment and hiring restrictions would carry real personal costs: senior officials would have to sell managed portfolios and companies would lose access to experienced former regulators, which backers of looser rules argue can make it harder to recruit qualified people from the private sector.

The public financing system and the new Office of Public Integrity would require ongoing federal spending, and the progressive tax on lobbying expenditures would face immediate legal challenges as a burden on political speech.

The bill had no cosponsors of either party and was introduced with less than two weeks left in the session, so there was no realistic path even to a hearing, much less negotiation over its most aggressive provisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core aims — ending congressional stock trading, closing the revolving door, and letting candidates run on small donations rather than corporate money — address problems that polling has consistently shown concern the public, and the bill includes workable mechanisms (a federal investment account for divested assets, published waivers) to soften the harsher edges. But the package is enormous and untested as a whole, it would require substantial new federal spending and enforcement machinery, and parts of it (the lobbying tax, broad hiring bans) would draw serious constitutional and practical challenges. Its immediate weakness was political: zero cosponsors and a two-week window meant it was symbolic from the day it was filed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced thirteen days before the session ended and referred to ten House committees; none of them acted, and the Congress expired with no hearing, no vote, and no action at all beyond the referral.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on December 20, 2022, with no cosponsors.

The same day, it was referred to ten House committees — Judiciary, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, Ways and Means, Financial Services, Intelligence, Rules, Foreign Affairs, Armed Services, and Budget — with scheduling left for the Speaker to determine later.
No committee took up the bill, no hearing or markup was scheduled, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without any further action.

The bill's provisions included a ban on stock ownership and trading by Members of Congress and senior officials, 2-to-6-year lobbying hiring bans, a corporate PAC ban, public campaign financing, and a new Office of Public Integrity to enforce ethics law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms, large banks and contractors, and incumbent officials keep the existing revolving-door, investment, and campaign finance rules untouched; nothing changed for anyone because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbyists and officeholders — the rules stayed the same

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 20, 2022, and served as its only sponsor.

against.name: Chairs of the ten referred committees
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill's provisions
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the two weeks remaining in the session.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; the referral left committee scheduling 'to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' and no scheduling ever followed.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only supporter in the record was its Democratic sponsor, and not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and political intelligence consultants
industries.note: The bill would bar former lobbyists from government jobs for 2–6 years, ban contingent-fee lobbying, tax lobbying expenditures progressively, and force political intelligence firms selling government information to investors to register under lobbying law. The industry's revenue model depends on the same access the bill restricts, so its gain would come at the public's cost of faith in government.

Companies over $150 billion in market cap or revenue could not hire senior officials for 4 years, faced civil penalties starting at 1 percent of net profit for violations, and former executives of companies under federal enforcement actions would be barred from agencies for 6 years. These rules exist to stop regulators and the regulated from trading places.

Contractors could not hire the officials who oversaw their contracts for 4 years, would fall under the Freedom of Information Act, and would have to publicly disclose their political spending. Disclosure and conflict rules make contracting decisions more accountable to taxpayers.

industries.industry: Corporate political donors and PAC operators
industries.note: Corporate PACs would be banned, corporations barred from fundraising for Members, foreign-owned corporations barred from election spending, and donors to tax-exempt political groups disclosed. The bill's public financing alternative is designed to shrink this group's influence over elections.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior executive officials
industries.note: Officeholders would have to divest individual stocks and derivatives, disclose 8 years of tax returns (President and Vice President), and face new recusal and post-employment rules. These restrictions run against officeholders' personal financial interests and in favor of constituents' ability to trust their decisions.

industries.industry: Think tanks, 501(c) nonprofits, and advocacy groups
industries.note: Groups that lobby would face expanded registration and donor-disclosure requirements, though the bill also repeals IRS limits on political-activity transparency. Larger politically active organizations would face the heaviest compliance costs; grassroots small-donor groups would see less impact.

Platforms would have to maintain political ad records, apply disclaimers to online political communications, and police foreign-national spending. Compliance costs would fall on the platforms while the transparency benefit goes to voters.
